label: remark on defini of resonances
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{remark on defini of resonances}
\ \ 

{\rm (1) It is clear that when $V\equiv0$, all thresholds $0,4,8,12$ are regular points of $H$. 

(2) Note that Nomura and Taira \cite[Theorem 1.7]{NT20} proved that, under the assumption $\beta>\frac{7}{2}$, any $\phi\in\ell^{2,-1}(\mathbb{Z}^3)$ satisfying $\phi+(-\Delta-\lambda\mp i0)^{-1}V\phi=0$ for $\lambda=4$ and $8$, necessarily belongs to $\phi\in\ell^2(\mathbb{Z}^3)$. Hence, no resonance occurs at the hyperbolic thresholds $4$ and $8$. 

(3) Moreover, by \eqref{proper of birmann operator}, for $\lambda\in\{4,8\}$, we have 
$$
\{\phi\in\ell^{2,-1}(\mathbb{Z}^3)\mid\phi+(-\Delta-\lambda\mp i0)^{-1}V\phi=0\}\subseteq\{\phi\in\ell^{2,-1}(\mathbb{Z}^3)\mid H\phi=\lambda\phi\}.
$$
However, the reverse inclusion does not hold in general.  Nevertheless, under suitable decay assumptions on $V$, they are equivalent when $\phi\in\ell^2(\mathbb Z^3)$. In this case, the eigenvalue condition in Definition \ref{defin of resonance types 4,8} can equivalently be replaced by the usual eigenvalue equation. We refer to Appendix \ref{example} for more details.

title: Remark
body_md:
{\rm (Embedded eigenvalue problem)}
    {\rm The absence of embedded eigenvalues is a natural spectral assumption in the above time-decay estimates, since such eigenvalues lead to singularities of the resolvent inside the continuous spectrum. 
    
 For discrete Schrödinger operators, this issue has drawn considerable interest and has been studied under stronger decay assumptions on the potential (see e.g. \cite{HHNO16,HMK22,HSSS12,IM14,Liu22,LMT25} and references therein). In particular, Isozaki and Morioka \cite{IM14} proved the absence of embedded eigenvalues for compactly supported potentials on $\mathbb{Z}^d$. More recently, Liu, Matos and Treuer \cite{LMT25} extended this conclusion to potentials decaying faster than any exponential, namely,
    $$
\limsup_{|n|\to\infty}\frac{\ln |V(n)|}{|n|}<-\gamma
\qquad\text{for every }\gamma>0.
$$
These results, however, do not directly cover the polynomial decay assumption imposed in this theorem. Thus, the absence of embedded eigenvalues remains an interesting problem for further investigation. 
 }

title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{Asymptotic expansion theorem 0}
 Let $H=-\Delta+V$ with $|V(n)|\lesssim \left<n\right>^{-\beta}$ for some $\beta>0$. Then the following asymptotic expansions hold in $\mathcal{B}(\sigma,-\sigma)$ as $|\omega|\rightarrow 0$ with $\arg\omega\in(0,2\pi)$.  
\begin{itemize}
\item[{\rm(1)}] If $0$ {\rm(}resp. $12${\rm)} is a regular point of $H$ and $\beta>3$, then for any $\sigma>\frac{3}{2}$, 
\begin{equation*}                               
R_V(\omega)=A_0-A_0vD_{0}vA_0+O(\omega^{\frac{1}{2}}),\quad
R_V(12-\omega)=\mathcal{A}_0-\mathcal{A}_0v\mathcal{D}_{0}v\mathcal{A}_0+O(\omega^{\frac{1}{2}}).
\end{equation*}
\item [{\rm(2)}] If $0$ {\rm(}resp. $12${\rm)} is a resonance of $H$ and $\beta>5$, then for any $\sigma>\frac{5}{2}$, 
\begin{equation*}                                 
R_V(\omega)=-A_0vS_1D_{1}S_1vA_0\omega^{-\frac{1}{2}}+O(1),\quad 
R_V(12-\omega)=-\mathcal{A}_0v\mathcal{S}_1\mathcal{D}_{1}\mathcal{S}_1v\mathcal{A}_0\omega^{-\frac{1}{2}}+O(1).
\end{equation*}
            
\item [{\rm(3)}] If $0$ {\rm(}resp. $12${\rm)} is an eigenvalue of $H$ and $\beta>7$, then for any $\sigma>\frac{7}{2}$, 
\begin{equation*}                               
R_V(\omega)=-A_0vS_2D_{2}S_2vA_0\omega^{-1}+O(\omega^{-\frac{1}{2}}),\quad R_V(12-\omega)=-\mathcal{A}_0v\mathcal{S}_2\mathcal{D}_{2}\mathcal{S}_2v\mathcal{A}_0\omega^{-1}+O(\omega^{-\frac{1}{2}}).
\end{equation*}
\end{itemize}
Here
\begin{itemize}
\item $D_0=(S+S_1)^{-1},\quad \mathcal{D}_0=(\mathcal{S}+\mathcal{S}_1)^{-1};$
    \vskip0.1cm
    \item $D_{1}=(S_1vA_1vS_1+S_2)^{-1}\ {\rm on} \ S_1\ell^2(\mathbb{Z}^3),\quad \mathcal{D}_{1}=(\mathcal{S}_1v\mathcal{A}_1v\mathcal{S}_1+\mathcal{S}_2)^{-1}\ {\rm on} \ \mathcal{S}_1\ell^2(\mathbb{Z}^3);$
    \vskip0.1cm
    \item $ D_{2}=(S_2vA_2vS_2)^{-1}\ {\rm on} \ S_2\ell^2(\mathbb{Z}^3),\quad\qquad\  \mathcal{D}_{2}=(\mathcal{S}_2v\mathcal{A}_2v\mathcal{S}_2)^{-1}\ {\rm on} \ \mathcal{S}_2\ell^2(\mathbb{Z}^3),$
\end{itemize}
and $A_0vS_2D_{2}S_2vA_0$ and $-\mathcal{A}_0v\mathcal{S}_2\mathcal{D}_{2}\mathcal{S}_2v\mathcal{A}_0$  
 are the orthogonal projections onto the eigenspaces of $H$ at $0$ and $12$, respectively. Moreover, these expansions are twice differentiable in $\mathcal{B}(\sigma,-\sigma)$ with $\sigma>\frac{5}{2}$.

title: Remark
body_md:
{\rm Note that when $\beta>1$, both $UvA_0v$ and $Uv\mathcal{A}_0v$ are compact operators on $\ell^2(\mathbb{Z}^3)$. Since  $U$ is invertible, it follows that 
    $US=I+UvA_0v$ and  $U\mathcal{S}=I+Uv\mathcal{A}_0v$
are Fredholm of index zero. Hence $$\dim(S_2\ell^2(\mathbb{Z}^3))\leq\dim(S_1\ell^2(\mathbb{Z}^3))<+\infty,\qquad\dim(\mathcal{S}_2\ell^2(\mathbb{Z}^3))\leq\dim(\mathcal{S}_1\ell^2(\mathbb{Z}^3))<+\infty.$$
Combining Definition \ref{defin of resonance types 0,12} with this lemma, we obtain the following characterization:
\begin{itemize}
\item $0$ is a regular point of $H$ $\Longleftrightarrow$
    $S_1\ell^2(\mathbb{Z}^3)=\{0\}$$\Longleftrightarrow$$S$ is invertible on $\ell^2(\mathbb{Z}^3)$.
\vskip0.1cm
\item 
    $0$ is a resonance of $H$ $\Longleftrightarrow$ $S_1\ell^2(\mathbb{Z}^3)\neq\{0\}$ but $S_2\ell^2(\mathbb{Z}^3)=\{0\}$$\Longleftrightarrow$ $S$ is not invertible on $\ell^2(\mathbb{Z}^3)$ but $S_1vA_1vS_1$ is invertible on $S_1\ell^2(\mathbb{Z}^3)$.
\vskip0.1cm
\item $0$ is an eigenvalue of $H$ $\Longleftrightarrow$ $S_2\ell^2(\mathbb{Z}^3)\neq\{0\}$$\Longleftrightarrow$ $S_1vA_1vS_1$ is not invertible on $S_1\ell^2(\mathbb{Z}^3)$. 
\end{itemize}
Thus, the successive invertibility conditions arising in the inversion
scheme precisely distinguish the regular, resonant, and eigenvalue cases
at the threshold.
}

title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lemm of expa}
{\rm (\cite[Lemma 2.1]{JN01})} Let $\mathcal{H}$ be a complex Hilbert space. Let $A$ be a closed operator and $P$ a projection. Suppose $A+P$ has a bounded inverse. Then $A$ has a bounded inverse if and only if
$$a\equiv P-P(A+P)^{-1}P$$
has a bounded inverse in $P\mathcal{H}$, and in this case
$$A^{-1}=(A+P)^{-1}+(A+P)^{-1}Pa^{-1}P(A+P)^{-1}.$$

body_md:
\label{remark of chara 4}
\ \

{\rm

(1)  Under the decay assumption of Lemma \ref{chara of solution and space 4}, there is no genuine resonance at the threshold $4$. Indeed, if
$f^\pm\in Q^\pm_1\ell^2(\mathbb{Z}^3)$, then by Lemma
\ref{chara of solution and space 4} there exists
$\phi^\pm\in\ell^{2,-1}(\mathbb{Z}^3)$ satisfying
$$\phi^{\pm}+(-\Delta-4\mp i0)^{-1}V\phi^{\pm}=0\quad {\rm and}\quad f^\pm=Uv\phi^\pm.$$
Lemma \ref{Taira lemma} (1) then implies that
$\phi^\pm\in\ell^2(\mathbb{Z}^3)$ and 
$\mathcal{F}(V\phi^\pm)|_{\mathcal{M}_4}=0.$
In particular, for $\xi_k:=\pi e_k\in\mathcal{M}_4$, $k=1,2,3$, we have
$$
\left<f^\pm,v_k\right>=(2\pi)^{\frac{3}{2}}\mathcal{F}\big(V\phi^\pm\big)\big(\xi_k\big)=0. 
$$
Hence, by the definition of $Q^\pm_2$, $Q^\pm_1\ell^2(\mathbb{Z}^3) = Q^\pm_2\ell^2(\mathbb{Z}^3).$ In other words, $Q_1^\pm vB_0^\pm vQ_1^\pm=0 $ on $Q_1^\pm\ell^2(\mathbb{Z}^3).$
\vskip0.1cm
(2) Consequently, combining Lemma
\ref{chara of solution and space 4}~(i) with Lemma
\ref{Taira lemma}~(1), the threshold $4$ admits only the regular and
eigenvalue cases. More precisely,
\begin{align}\label{char of Q1pm}
\begin{split}
Q^{\pm}_1\ell^2(\mathbb{Z}^3)&=\{0\} \Longleftrightarrow\phi+(-\Delta-4\mp i0)^{-1}V\phi=0 \ \text{has only the zero solution in }\ell^{2,-1}(\mathbb{Z}^3),\\
Q^{\pm}_1\ell^2(\mathbb{Z}^3)&\neq\{0\} \Longleftrightarrow\phi+(-\Delta-4\mp i0)^{-1}V\phi=0 \ \text{has non-zero solution in }\ell^{2}(\mathbb{Z}^3).
\end{split}
\end{align}
Moreover, Lemma \ref{chara of solution and space 4}~(ii) shows that the
two a priori different classifications arising from the upper and lower
half-plane boundary values coincide.

Arguing as at the threshold $0$, $Q^\pm$ is a Fredholm operator of index zero, and hence
$Q^\pm$ is invertible if and only if $\ker Q^\pm=\{0\}$. Combining this with \eqref{char of Q1pm} and Definition
\ref{defin of resonance types 4,8}, we obtain
\begin{itemize}
    \item 
    $4$ is a regular point of $H$ $\Longleftrightarrow$ $Q^+$ is invertible on $\ell^2(\mathbb{Z}^3)$ $\Longleftrightarrow$ $Q^-$ is invertible on $\ell^2(\mathbb{Z}^3)$.
\vskip0.1cm
\item $4$ is an eigenvalue of $H$ $\Longleftrightarrow$ $Q^+$ is not invertible on $\ell^2(\mathbb{Z}^3)$$\Longleftrightarrow$ $Q^-$ is not invertible on $\ell^2(\mathbb{Z}^3)$. 
\end{itemize}  
\begin{comment}
                                                                                                                                                                                             
                 
                                                                     
               
                                                                                    
\end{comment}
}

title: Proof
body_md:
First, taking $N=0$ and letting $\omega=\pm i\varepsilon$ with $\varepsilon>0$ in \eqref{expan at 4}, we have 
\begin{equation*}
E^{\pm}_0=\lim\limits_{\varepsilon\rightarrow0,\ \varepsilon>0}R_0(4\pm i\varepsilon)\quad in\ \mathcal{B}(s,-s),\quad s>7/2.
\end{equation*}
Then it follows that ${E}^{\pm}_0=(-\Delta-4\mp i0)^{-1}$ on $\ell^{2,s}(\mathbb{Z}^3)$ for $s>7/2.$
\vskip0.1cm
{\bf\underline{(i)}} ``$\bm{\Longrightarrow}$" Let $f^{\pm}\in Q^{\pm}_1{\ell^2(\mathbb{Z}^3)}$. Then $(U+vE^{\pm}_0v)f^{\pm}=Q^{\pm}f^{\pm}=0.$ Multiplying both sides by $U$, we obtain
$f^{\pm}=-UvE^{\pm}_0vf^{\pm}$. Since $\beta>7$, we have $vf^{\pm}\in \ell^{2,s}(\mathbb{Z}^3)\subseteq\ell^{2,1}(\mathbb{Z}^3)$ for some $7/2<s\leq\beta/{2}$. Using
$(-\Delta-4\mp i0)^{-1}\in\mathcal{B}(1,-1)$, we may therefore define $$\phi^{\pm}:=-E^{\pm}_0vf^{\pm}=-(-\Delta-4\mp i0)^{-1}vf^{\pm}\in\ell^{2,-1}(\mathbb{Z}^3).$$ Then,
$f^{\pm}=Uv\phi^{\pm}$ and $vf^{\pm}=V\phi^{\pm}$, so that
$\phi^{\pm}+(-\Delta-4\mp i0)^{-1}V\phi^{\pm}=0.$ 
\vskip0.1cm
``$\bm{\Longleftarrow}$" Suppose that there exists $\phi^{\pm}\in \ell^{2,-1}(\mathbb{Z}^3)$ satisfying the equation $$\phi^{\pm}+(-\Delta-4\mp i0)^{-1}V\phi^{\pm}=0.$$
Let $f^{\pm}:=Uv\phi^{\pm}\in\ell^2(\mathbb{Z}^3)$. Then $vf^{\pm}=V\phi^{\pm}\in\ell^{2,s}(\mathbb{Z}^3)$ for some $7/2<s\leq \beta-1$. Therefore, $$\phi^{\pm}=-(-\Delta-4\mp i0)^{-1}V\phi^{\pm}=-E^{\pm}_0vf^{\pm}.$$
Hence 
 $Q^{\pm}f^{\pm}=(U+vE^{\pm}_0v)f^{\pm}=v\phi^{\pm}-v\phi^{\pm}=0,$
which yields $f^{\pm}\in Q^{\pm}_1\ell^2(\mathbb{Z}^3)$.
\vskip0.1cm
{\bf\underline{(ii)}} For any $f\in Q^+_1\ell^2(\mathbb{Z}^3)$, it follows from (i) that there exists $\phi\in\ell^{2,-1}(\mathbb{Z}^3)$ such that $$\phi+(-\Delta-4- i0)^{-1}V\phi=0\ \ \text{and}\ \ f=Uv\phi.$$ Applying Lemma \ref{Taira lemma} (1) to $\phi$, we obtain $\mathcal{F}(V\phi)\big|_{\mathcal{M}_4}=0$. Since $V\phi\in\ell^{2,s}(\mathbb{Z}^3)$ for some $s>\frac{7}{2}$, $\mathcal{F}(V\phi)\in C^1(\mathbb{T}^3)$ by the Sobolev embedding theorem. By Lemma \ref{Taira lemma} (2), we have
\begin{equation*}
    (\mathcal{M}(x)-4\mp i0)^{-1}\mathcal{F}(V\phi)(x)=(\mathcal{M}(x)-4)^{-1}\mathcal{F}(V\phi)(x).
\end{equation*}
This implies that $E^+_0vf=E^+_0V\phi=E^-_0V\phi=E^-_0vf$. Thus, $f\in Q^-_1\ell^2(\mathbb{Z}^3)$ follows from 
$$Q^-f=(U+vE^-_0v)f=Uf+vE^+_0vf=Q^+f=0.$$
Similarly, we can prove $Q^-_1\ell^2(\mathbb{Z}^3)\subseteq Q^+_1\ell^2(\mathbb{Z}^3)$. Hence, $Q^+_1\ell^2(\mathbb{Z}^3)=Q^-_1\ell^2(\mathbb{Z}^3)$ is established. This completes the proof.

title: Proof
body_md:
We first verify that $F_0^\pm$ and $F_2^\pm$ are well-defined. Since $(E^+_0)^*=E^-_0$, we have $(Q^\pm)^*=Q^\mp$. By Lemma
\ref{chara of solution and space 4} (ii), $$\operatorname{Ker}(Q^{\pm})^{*}=\operatorname{Ker}Q^{\mp}=\operatorname{Ran}Q^{\mp}_1=\operatorname{Ran}Q^{\pm}_1=\operatorname{Ker}Q^{\pm}.$$ Moreover, $Q^\pm$ is a Fredholm operator
of index zero and hence has closed range. Therefore, Remark
\ref{remark of invertibility} implies that   $F^{\pm}_0=(Q^{\pm}+Q^\pm_1)^{-1}$ is well-defined.

It remains to consider $F^{\pm}_2= \left(Q_2^\pm vE_1^\pm vQ_2^\pm\right)^{-1}$.  Since $Q^\pm$ is Fredholm, $Q_1^\pm$, and hence $Q_2^\pm$, is of finite
rank. Thus it suffices to prove injectivity. Let $f^\pm\in Q_2^\pm\ell^2(\mathbb{Z}^3)$. By Remark
\ref{remark of chara 4}, $\mathcal{F}(vf^\pm)\big|_{\mathcal{M}_4}=0.$ 
Moreover, the decay of $v$ implies
$vf^\pm\in\ell^{2,s}(\mathbb{Z}^3)$ for some $s>\frac52$, and hence
$\mathcal{F}(vf^\pm)\in C^1(\mathbb{T}^3)$. Lemma \ref{Taira lemma}~(2) therefore gives
$$ (\mathcal{M}(x)-4)^{-1}\mathcal{F}(vf^\pm)\in L^2(\mathbb{T}^3).$$
Proceeding as in the proof of the injectivity of $S_2vA_2vS_2$ at the
threshold $0$, we conclude that
$Q_2^\pm vE_1^\pm vQ_2^\pm$ is injective and hence invertible on
$Q_2^\pm\ell^2(\mathbb{Z}^3)$. Therefore $F_2^\pm$ is well-defined.

\vskip0.1cm
We next turn to the inversion of
$$M^{\pm}(4+\omega):=U+vR^{\pm}_0(4+\omega)v, \qquad \pm\operatorname{Im}\omega>0.$$ 
Using $Q_1^\pm vB_0^\pm vQ_1^\pm=0$, and applying the same iterative inversion scheme as at the threshold $0$, we obtain
\begin{itemize}
    \item If 4 is a regular point of $H$ and $\beta>7$, then 
\begin{equation}\label{asy expan regu 4}
(M^{\pm}(4+\omega))^{-1}=F^\pm_{0}-F^\pm_{0}vB^\pm_0vF^\pm_{0}\omega^{\frac{1}{2}}+F^\pm_0O(\omega)F^\pm_0, \quad|\omega|\rightarrow0,\quad\pm\operatorname{Im} \omega>0.
\end{equation}
\item If 4 is an eigenvalue of $H$ and $\beta>11$, then 
\begin{equation}\label{asy expan 2nd 4}
(M^{\pm}(4+\omega))^{-1}=Q^\pm_2F^\pm_{2}Q^\pm_2\omega^{-1}+O(\omega^{-\frac{1}{2}}),\quad|\omega|\rightarrow0,\quad\pm\operatorname{Im} \omega>0.
\end{equation}
\end{itemize} 
Hence, combining these expansions with \eqref{rela betw RV and inver of Mw}, we obtain the corresponding expansions for $R^\pm_V(4+\omega)$. 
By combining the derivative estimates for the free resolvent in \cite[Corollary 2.10]{Kop09} with the above inversion argument, the expansions in Proposition \ref{Asymptotic expansion theorem 4} can be differentiated twice in $\mathcal{B}(\sigma,-\sigma)$ for $\sigma>\frac{11}{2}$.

Moreover, by Remark \ref{remark on defini of resonances} and the argument used in the proof of Proposition \ref{Asymptotic expansion theorem 0}, we can also show that $E^{\pm}_0vQ^{\pm}_2F^{\pm}_2Q^{\pm}_2vE^{\pm}_0$ is the eigenprojection of $H$ associated with the eigenvalue $4$. This completes the proof.

label: mourre estimate free
title: Proof
body_md:
Under the Fourier transform $\mathcal{F}_d$ on $\mathbb{Z}^d$:
\begin{equation*}
    (\mathcal{F}_d\phi)(x):=(2\pi)^{-d/2}\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}^d}^{}e^{-in\cdot x}\phi(n), \quad \phi\in\ell^2(\mathbb{Z}^d),
\end{equation*}
it suffices to prove the corresponding Mourre estimate on
$L^2((-\pi,\pi]^d)$. Set
$$\mathcal{H}:=\mathcal{H}_0+\mathcal{V},\qquad \mathcal{V}:=\mathcal{F}_d V\mathcal{F}_d^{-1},\qquad \mathcal{A}:=\mathcal{F}_d A\mathcal{F}^{-1}_d,$$ where
\begin{equation*}
\mathcal{H}_0:=\mathcal{F}_d (-\Delta_{\mathbb{Z}^d})\mathcal{F}^{-1}_d=2\big(d-\sum\limits_{j=1}^{d}{\rm cos}x_j\big)=:h(x),
\end{equation*}
and 
\begin{equation*}
  \mathcal{A}=\sum\limits_{j=1}^{d}(2i{\rm sin}x_j\partial_{x_j}+i{\rm cos}x_j-{\rm sin}x_j).
\end{equation*}
We first establish the Mourre estimate for $\mathcal{H}_0$. Let  $\lambda\in(0,4d)\setminus\{4j\}^{d-1}_{j=1}$. A direct computation gives
\begin{equation*}
[\mathcal{H}_0,i\mathcal{A}]=4\sum\limits_{j=1}^{d}({\rm sin}x_j)^2=|\nabla h(x)|^2.
 \end{equation*}
Let 
 $M_{\lambda}=\{x\in(-\pi,\pi]^d:h(x)=\lambda\}.$ Since $\lambda$ is not a threshold, $\nabla h(x)\neq0$ on
$M_\lambda$. Moreover, $M_\lambda$ is compact, and therefore
$$
C(\lambda)
:=
\inf_{x\in M_\lambda}|\nabla h(x)|^2
>0.
$$
Choose $0<\eta<C(\lambda)$. By continuity, there exists
$\varepsilon>0$ such that
$$
|\nabla h(x)|^2
\geq C(\lambda)-\eta,
\qquad
x\in h^{-1}([\lambda-\varepsilon,\lambda+\varepsilon]).
$$
Hence, with $I=(\lambda-\varepsilon,\lambda+\varepsilon)$, we obtain
\begin{equation}\label{mourre estimate free}
E_{\mathcal{H}_0}(I)
[\mathcal{H}_0,i\mathcal{A}]
E_{\mathcal{H}_0}(I)
\geq
\big(C(\lambda)-\eta\big)E_{\mathcal{H}_0}(I).
\end{equation}
We next pass from $\mathcal{H}_0$ to $\mathcal{H}$. Since
$V(n)\to0$ as $|n|\to\infty$, $V$ is compact on $\ell^2(\mathbb{Z}^d)$,
and hence $\mathcal{V}$ is compact on $L^2((-\pi,\pi]^d)$. It follows that
$E_{\mathcal{H}}(I)-E_{\mathcal{H}_0}(I)$ is compact. Moreover, let \begin{equation*}
\widetilde{A}=A-\frac{i}{2}\sum\limits_{j=1}^{d}(P_j-P^*_j)=\frac{i}{2}\sum\limits_{j=1}^{d}\big((P^*_j-P_j)N_j+N_j(P^*_j-P_j)\big),\quad \Phi(x)=-\sum\limits_{j=1}^{d}{\rm sin}x_j.
\end{equation*}
Denote $\widetilde{\mathcal{A}}=\mathcal{F}_d\widetilde{A}\mathcal{F}^{-1}_d$. Since 
$[V,i\widetilde{A}]$ is compact on $\ell^2(\mathbb{Z}^d)$ (cf. \cite[Page 17]{Man17}), it follows that
$$[\mathcal{V},i\mathcal{A}]=[\mathcal{V},i\widetilde{\mathcal{A}}]+[\mathcal{V},i\Phi]=\mathcal{F}_d[V,i\widetilde{A}]\mathcal{F}^{-1}_d+[\mathcal{V},i\Phi]$$
is compact on $L^2((-\pi,\pi]^d)$. Combining these facts with \eqref{mourre estimate free} and the decompositions
$$E_{\mathcal{H}}(I)=E_{\mathcal{H}_0}(I)+E_{\mathcal{H}}(I)-E_{\mathcal{H}_0}(I),\quad [\mathcal{H},i\mathcal{A}]=[\mathcal{H}_0,i\mathcal{A}]+[\mathcal{V},i\mathcal{A}],$$
we obtain the desired estimates.
